newsitem.title: FRANCE: French union wants "negotiating" job conference.
newsitem.headline: French union wants "negotiating" job conference.

text.p: The head of the French FO trade union leader, Marc Blondel, said on Tuesday that a national conference on work, jobs and wages proposed by Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin should have to lead to genuine talks with employers.
Blondel also said he would like to see the government set a deadline for reaching agreement on a 35-hour week, but this shift was unlikely to occur uniformly.
"I'm for the 35-hour week, but I know in advance we won't get there in the same fashion in every sector," Blondel said.
"Reducing work time in the production sector for example is is not the same thing as reducing work time in retail."

"I believe there should be a date by which the 35 hours should be reached, but it should be left to economic sectors themselves to deal with the practical aspects, for example in sectors where public opening hours are involved," he said in a telephone interview.

France's new prime minister, Socialist Lionel Jospin, has pledged to push for a 35-hour week, instead of 39, but laid the emphasis on getting there by consensus and he has also proposed a national conference of employers and unions to dicuss jobs, wages and work time organisation.
"I believe above all that a deadline date should be fixed (for agreements to move to 35-hours)," Blondel said.
The ideal would be to have it as fast as possible, but he did not expect it to happen much faster than the three years within which Jospin hopes to get there.

Blondel said he would make the case for wage rises at the national conference -- for which a starting date has yet to be set -- but that success in the private sector depended on talks between unions and employers, not directly on the government.

"The prime minister is in charge when it comes to the SMIC (minimum wage). The prime minister is in charge when it comes to unemployment benefits for those who no longer claim on the dole system and he is also responsible for his own staff, the civil service," Blondel said. "But it does not rest with him in the private sector. In the private sector, it's with private employers that we negotiate."

Speaking about the civil service, he said the outgoing centre-right government had unilaterally imposed a 1997 pay rise that had been and still was opposed by unions and the problem would not simply evaporate.
Blondel took a far more cautious line on calls, primarily from the Communist-led CGT union, for a significant rise in the national minimum wage (the SMIC).

"We have some problems with the SMIC. There's a whole series of sectors where there's relief on social security contributions for SMIC wages, which means that the more we raise the SMIC the less we see in income for the social security system," he said.
"I'm all for increasing purchasing power, but we cannot raise people's purchasing power if the real effect ends up being yet another indirect hand for employers."
